variants.intro: **TAG:** Engine Variants **H2:** M103 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car? The M103 was produced in two displacements (2.6L and 3.0L) with multiple sub-codes indicating specific applications and emissions configurations. The differences are significant when buying a replacement engine. #### M103.940 - 2.6L, W201 190 E 2.6 & W124 260 E (1985-1993) - **Fitted to:** W201 190 E 2.6 (1985-1993), W124 260 E (1985-1992), W126 260 SE/SEL - **Key technical difference:** 2,597 cc displacement, 82.9 mm bore, 80.25 mm stroke, CIS-E fuel injection, 158-166 hp depending on catalyst - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family timing chain stretch and oil leak patterns - **Interchange note:** Not a straight swap with 3.0L variants - ECU, injectors and some ancillaries differ. However, 2.6 to 3.0 swaps are accessible as CIS-E components are shared except for the ECU #### M103.950 - 2.6L, W124 260 E (catalyst/non-catalyst variants) - **Fitted to:** W124 260 E, C124 260 E Coupé - **Key technical difference:** Similar to M103.940, 2,597 cc, 160-166 hp depending on catalyst fitment, specific ECU calibration for W124 application - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family oil leak and timing chain patterns - **Interchange note:** Interchangeable with M103.940 in same chassis with ECU matching - verify ECU compatibility before fitting #### M103.960 - 3.0L, W126 300 SE/SEL & R107 300 SL (1985-1989) - **Fitted to:** W126 300 SE / 300 SEL, R107 300 SL (1985-1989) - **Key technical difference:** 2,962 cc displacement, 88.5 mm bore, 80.25 mm stroke, 180-188 hp depending on catalyst, specific ECU calibration for S-Class/SL applications - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family timing chain stretch pattern; higher torque output may accelerate chain wear on high-mileage examples - **Interchange note:** Not a straight swap with 2.6L variants - ECU, injectors, air box and some ancillaries differ. Requires full ECU and fuel system matching #### M103.980 - 3.0L, W124 300 E & R129 300 SL (1985-1993) - **Fitted to:** W124 300 E, C124 300 CE, R129 300 SL (1989-1993) - **Key technical difference:** 2,962 cc, 180-190 hp, CIS-E fuel injection, heart-shaped combustion chamber on later examples - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family timing chain and oil leak patterns; early (1985) non-catalyst version produced 188 hp at 5,700 rpm with 10:1 compression - **Interchange note:** Not a straight swap with 2.6L variants - ECU, injectors and air box differ. Post-1989 variants have improved combustion chamber design - verify compatibility before fitting between generations #### M103.984 / .987 - 3.0L, R129 300 SL & W463 300 GE - **Fitted to:** R129 300 SL (1989-1993), W463 300 GE (1990-1997) - **Key technical difference:** 2,962 cc, 170-190 hp depending on application, specific ECU calibration for SL and G-Class applications, different ancillaries for off-road use - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family oil leak and timing chain patterns; G-Class application may see additional cooling system stress from off-road use - **Interchange note:** Not a straight swap with saloon variants - engine mounts, ancillaries and some cooling system components differ. Always match the application when buying a replacement

mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes M103 engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned M103 supply-only costs approximately £1,500-£2,500, with fitted prices ranging from £1,880 to £3,300 depending on labour rates. Used units start at £800-£1,500, and full rebuilds run from £2,500-£4,000. Prices are supply-only; fitting adds 10-14 hours at independent specialist rates. Warranty varies: 3-6 months on used, 12-24 months on reconditioned and rebuilt.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common failures on the M103?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most documented issues are timing chain stretch (causing poor performance and potential chain jump), oil leaks from valve stem seals, crankshaft seals and timing cover, and clogged injectors (CIS-E fuel system). These issues are age-related rather than mileage-related and affect virtually all M103s as they age. Timing chain replacement is strongly advised at 80k-150k miles. Valve stem seals degrade over time; replacement restores performance and reduces oil consumption. Injector cleaning or replacement addresses poor running and rough idle.

mainEntity.name: Which Mercedes models use the M103 engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The M103 was fitted to a wide range of Mercedes models between 1985-1993: W201 190 E 2.6, W124 260 E / 300 E, W126 260 SE/SEL / 300 SE/SEL, R107 300 SL, R129 300 SL (1989-1993), and W463 300 GE. Two displacements: 2.6L (158-166 hp) and 3.0L (180-190 hp). The M104 successor replaced the M103 from 1990 onwards.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used or reconditioned M103 engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: A used M103 can be viable for lower-value classic Mercedes models, but only if it has documented proof of recent timing chain and oil seal work. Without that, factor in £1,000-£2,000 for preventative work (chain, seals, gaskets). A reconditioned engine is the safer choice - it includes new timing chain, valve stem seals, gaskets and injector service, with a 12-24 month warranty. Used is cheaper (£800-£1,500) but age-related issues are significant. Reconditioned addresses all known weak points and gives peace of mind.

mainEntity.name: How do I confirm which M103 variant my car has?

acceptedAnswer.text: Check the engine code stamped on a metal plate on the left-hand side of the block, above the oil filter housing. The code will be in the format '103.xxx' followed by the serial number. The V5C logbook also lists the full engine number. 940 / 950: 2.6L variants (158-166 hp). 960 / 980: 3.0L variants (180-190 hp). The 984 / 987 variants are used in R129 SL and W463 G-Class applications.

mainEntity.name: How long does an M103 engine typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With proper maintenance, these engines are legendary for their durability - well-maintained examples regularly exceed 500,000 km (310,000 miles). The SOHC design is simple and robust; the limiting factors are the timing chain and oil seals. Timing chain replacement is recommended at 80k-150k miles. Regular oil changes (5,000-8,000 miles) with Mercedes-spec oil are essential. Valve stem seals degrade with age - replacement restores performance and reduces oil consumption.
